blocks.text: InNNEWS-Indonesia is refaced with data that should shake government awareness. PISA 2022, which measures math, reading and science skills, puts Indonesia at 369. This makes Indonesia the lowest group in the world and only superior to countries like Cambodia that record 337, or Dominican 350. In Southeast Asia alone, the Indonesian position is very alarming. Singapore goes to 560, Vietnam 468, Malaysia 404, and Thailand 379. The distance between Indonesia and the neighboring countries is no longer thin; it's wide-open, showing that there's something wrong at the foundation of our education.

When other countries move forward, Indonesia seems to be far behind. China records 535, Japan 533, South Korea 523, Estonia 524, and Canada 516. In a global landscape like this, Indonesia scores not only low; it is a marker that this country does not prepare its youth to compete in the future. Tren PISA Indonesia during 2012. 2022 also shows a decline, especially in math that once touched 391 and now slumps to 359. This drop goes on in secret, for years, without a serious government response.

The biggest problem is not in the ability of Indonesian children, but in the system that the country is building. When the curriculum changes like changing heads, when teachers are burdened by administration instead of being supported by teaching, when the learning facility is unequal between the city and the village, there's no way we're expecting PISA scores to rise. The international result was not a good understanding of intentions, but it was a judgment of the reality that occurs every day in an Indonesian classroom.

What's more concerning is that government attitudes tend to underestimate the depth of this problem. Instead of treating PISA data as a national alarm, the government is responding often with a normal statement: evaluation will be done, curriculum adjusted, competition-reinforcing program executed. However, from 560 Singapore to 369 Indonesia, or from 468 Vietnam to our position, it is clear that the government's response has not touched the root of the problem. The neighboring countries proved that the changing quality of education can happen when teachers are reinforced, the ecosystem of learning is built, and policy doesn't change like seasonal advertising.

The cost of unseriousness is not borne by cabinet or ministry, but by millions of students who are about to enter the workforce with fragile literacy skills and inadequate numeration skills. They will compete in a global market filled with talent from countries whose foundations are 100 to 150 points above Indonesia. And when that happens, our loss is not just statistics, it's the reality of life: low productivity, dependence on foreign labor, and the loss of young economic opportunity.

We need national honesty to admit that Indonesia is on the wrong track. Changes cannot be done with tambal- flam policy or rhetoric optimism. We need a big investment in teachers, stability curriculum, family literature, to nutrition and child health. We need a government that's ready to admit that our education foundation is fragile and has to be amplified, not wrapped in a successful claim.

The world is running. Singapore was not only 191 points above Indonesia; it was in a different educational galaxy. In Vietnam, which two decades ago saw Indonesia as a giant Southeast Asia, now adrift almost 100 points. If the government doesn't take extraordinary steps, Indonesia will only be a large nation in population, but small in global rival power.

It's time for the government to abandon the comfort of rhetoric and face the harsh realities of those numbers. We're running out of time. Without radical and measurable change, the future of Indonesia will be left behind long before we can catch up.
